records.text: Fork deployed! One attacker hits several targets at the same time.
Alert! A fork is now available to the other side: one of their pieces can strike several targets at a stroke. Locate that piece, first priority.
Another move had a fork primed, one attacker on several targets together. This move never gives the order.
Pinned to the king and held at its post. That piece can't leave the line without exposing its own king.
Status report: the other side has a pin to the king in reach. Once pinned, it can't leave that line without exposing the king.
Another move could have pinned a piece to its king and held it there. That piece would have been frozen at its post, unable to leave the line without exposing the king. Opportunity declined.
Skewer on target! Attack the front piece, and once it clears the line, the rear piece is exposed. Textbook.
Watch the line! A skewer opens for the other side: when the front piece moves, the piece behind it could be exposed.
Loaded skewer, sitting in a stronger move. Drive off the front piece, and the rear one is exposed. This move passes on that order.
Target the defender. Capture it, and its ward stands unprotected. Standard procedure.
Defender in the open! The other side can capture it, and whatever it guards could end up unprotected. Check its duties now.
Another move could have captured a defender and stripped the protection from what it guarded. Not this time.
Back rank, and the king's own troops are the walls. That's the mating pattern, and it works!
Back rank under threat! The other side gets a route to mate there, with the king trapped behind its own pieces.
A back-rank mate was ready, with the king hemmed in by its own troops. This move stands down instead.
The mission is promotion: a pawn reaches the last rank and earns a new rank as a piece. Track its route up the board.
Eyes on that pawn! The other side gets a shot at promotion. Track its route to the last rank.
A stronger move sent a pawn toward the last rank to promote. This move leaves it waiting in the ranks.
Discovered attack, launched! The blocker moves off, and the piece behind it goes on the attack. Two units in action off a single order.
Heads up! A discovered attack is now available to the other side. Watch for a piece of theirs stepping aside to unleash the one behind it.
Another move carried a discovered attack: step one piece aside, and the one behind it goes to work. This move doesn't give that order.
Double attack deployed! Two fronts, one order, and both demand an answer.
Two-front warning! A double attack opens for the other side, two threats at once. Find both before any reply.
Two fronts at once: that's what a stronger move had. This one stays on a single front.
Deflection executed! Draw the defender off its post, and whatever it was covering is left open.
Posts under pressure! The other side can pull a defender away with a deflection, and what it guards could be left open.
There was a defender to draw off its post in another move. That deflection never gets ordered.
Unguarded piece, captured. No defender, no problem. Target collected.
Another move could have captured an undefended piece, and this one goes right past it. Sweep for unguarded pieces first.
Sentry missing! A piece stands with no defender, and the other side can take it.
Hold the post! This move pulls a piece's only effective defender off duty, and the other side can take what it was guarding.
Unanswered threat! The opponent's last move set it up, and now a piece can be captured. Every threat gets an answer.
Full count on that exchange! This capture lets the other side recapture something worth more. That trade costs the mover.
Minor piece deployed off the back rank. Another unit on duty!
Another move would have called a minor piece up from its starting square.
The rook holds an open file, cleared of every pawn. Clear road ahead.
Another move would have handed a rook an open file, empty of pawns.
The rook is posted on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns stand on it, but at least one enemy pawn does.
With another move, a rook would have had a semi-open file: no pawns of its own color on it, at least one enemy pawn ahead.
A passed pawn on the field! The road ahead is free of enemy pawns, on its own file and either neighbor. Note it on the map.
Another move had a passed pawn on offer, with no enemy pawns ahead on its file or either flank.
Forward march! The passed pawn was already free, and now it's one square closer.
Another move would have sent the passed pawn on another advance.
Isolation: a pawn with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. No backup on its flanks.
Another move would have cut a pawn off from support on both flanks: isolated.
Reinforcements! A piece with no guard just got one.
Another move would have sent a defender to a piece that had none.
No guard on this piece now. That alone doesn't mean it can be won, but keep watch.
Another move would have stripped a piece of its defender, which alone wouldn't mean it could be won.
New exit for the king, a legal square it lacked a move ago. Always worth having.
Another move would have given the king a fresh exit.
Castling complete! The king and rook both move in a single turn. Formation set.
The alternative was castling, which moves king and rook together in one turn.
One capture, and that bishop pair is finished. The side that lost the bishop no longer has one on each square color.
Another move would have taken a bishop and split the opposing bishop pair.
Doubled pawns on the field: same color, same file, one in front of the other.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, one stacked ahead of the other on a single file.
Priority alert. This move leaves the king open to a forced checkmate. Retrace the attack and find where the defense broke.
Forced checkmate was available, and this move stands down. Back to that position. Find the finish.
Sacrifice on the board, and it holds. Even accepted, the sacrifice survives the line we checked.
Last line of defense. This was the lone move we checked that stayed playable; every other choice lost.
Only this move kept the advantage among the ones we checked; all the others lost. Mission-critical.
Incoming! An immediate capture is waiting for the other side. Inspect that reply first.
Incoming check: that's the strongest reply. The king gets defended before anything else.
The engine has a different move at the top of its orders. Set it up and compare the replies.
This costs value next to the engine's best. Check the reply and see what gave way.
Engine report: strong, very little value left behind.
Sound move, solid footing. The engine's first choice is elsewhere, but this keeps most of the position's value.
Opening move on record. Standard drill.
End of the manual: the game leaves our opening book here. From now on, it's open country.
Back in the fight! Playable again, and this move did it after the earlier setback.
The setback is repaired, with help from the other side's errors. Take the reinforcements.
Chance seized! The opponent's last move offered an opening, and this move went straight for it.
The opponent's last move offered a chance, and this move overlooks it. Back to that moment for the right response.
Same issue, earlier in this game. Line those moments up and find the common weak spot.
Support restored! That piece left unguarded earlier is back under guard.
Another small concession logged. Together with the earlier ones, they've worn the position down. Review the whole sequence.
The edge was held through to the win! Review that stretch and see how it was done.
The same issue shows up in other saved games. Put them on the study list together.
Checkmate, mission complete! The king is surrounded, with no legal way out.
Checkmate, and the king is boxed in. Regroup and find where the defense could have held.
Draw declared. The result stands, but the earlier decisions still deserve an inspection.
Survey the board, then make your move when ready.
Negative. Reset and try another move.
That attempt didn't report back. Run it again.
Saved engine analysis reports a forced checkmate for the side that played this move.
Saved engine analysis flags a forced checkmate for the other side once this move is played.
At the end of the saved line, the side that played this move is ahead on material compared with the start.
At the end of the saved line, the side that played this move is behind on material compared with the start.
Clearance granted for this exercise. The moves shown don't reveal a clear tactical reason, and none is invented here.
Not cleared for this exercise. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves, so try another.
Match confirmed: the move is on this exercise's saved list. Those saved answers set what passes.
Not on this exercise's saved-answer list. Off the list doesn't mean off the mark: another legal move can still be reasonable.
Inspect the move. Next position after that.
Top work! The reason behind it goes in the kit too.
Practice logged, schedule untouched.
Solved, and logged. This one stays on the relearning list.
Starting position, before any moves.
Next move up. Note what changes.
Check on the king! That gets dealt with first.
The king gets clear of check.
Promoted! The pawn earns its new rank on the last row.
Promotion on the last rank, with check.
The pawn promotes on the last rank with checkmate. The king is boxed in for good.
Promotion on the last rank, and the promoting side's king is out of check.
Capture made. One piece leaves the board.
Capture, plus check.
A capture that's also checkmate. Every escape route is closed.
A capture, and check is lifted from the king.
Capture and promotion on the last rank, all in one move.
One pawn captures, promotes on the last rank and gives check. Busy soldier!
One pawn captures, promotes and mates. Every square around that king is denied.
A pawn capture on the last rank brings promotion, and its king is out of check too.
Castling, and the rook gives check on arrival.
Castling delivers checkmate, and the king is cut off from every legal square.
One attacker hits several targets, then takes one. This example also ends with a material gain for that side.
That piece can't capture. The pin to its king holds it: leave the line, and the king is exposed.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece has no free retreat, so any escape has to keep the king shielded.
The defenders are pinned to their king and can't recapture. Capture confirmed, and the line shown gains material.
Eyes on the pinned piece. Its king would be exposed if it left the line, and these moves capture it.
Once the front piece gets out of the way, the piece behind it is captured on the same line.
Check pushes the king aside, and then the attacker claims what stood behind.
The lone defender is taken out first, and its charge follows.
The defender is lured off its post, and its abandoned piece is captured.
The blocker moves, the line opens, and the capture comes from the piece behind it.
A piece clears the way, and the one behind it gives check.
Double check, two checking pieces at once!
The first piece attacks and uncovers a second attacker. The capture comes from that second piece.
Promotion, and the example finishes with that side up material.
Captured: one undefended piece, and by the end of the example the capturing side is up material.
A relative pin used to hold the attacking piece. The opponent's last move ended it, the target sat still, and the line shown takes it.
The other side has the reply marked on the board. Play it and see what follows.
Before moving, inspect your pieces for any that can be captured with no useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, scan for undefended enemy pieces.
Check forcing moves for a single attacker that hits two valuable targets.
Before moving a pinned piece, check what it's guarding behind it: the king, or a bigger asset.
Past the first target, keep scanning. A line attack can hit what's standing behind.
Before trading off a defender, confirm what it's protecting.
When a blocking piece moves, see what line it opens.
Hunt for one order that opens two fronts. A check or a freshly opened line counts as a front.
Before moving a back-rank defender, secure an escape square for your king.
Count the moves to promotion, and look at which pawn pushes force a response.
A defender on the move leaves something uncovered. Check what, before it goes.
Tally both halves of the exchange: what you take, and what comes back.
Check whether a forcing exchange can pull a defender off another duty.
In this exercise, the saved answers give the orders. Moves outside them aren't automatically mistakes.
Here is one way play could go if the replies are strong. Not all of those replies are forced.
Material changes cover only the line shown, counted from its start. The written explanation names the piece values used in that count.
The saved line doesn't establish a simple tactical reason, and no positional reason is claimed. March through it and weigh every reply.
The answer policy saved for this exercise governs this explanation. Check the written notes for the setting in use.
Here are the moves of your study line, in order.
Confirmed: part of your study material.
Your move should come from the study lines you selected.
A move from any of your selected opening lines counts.
Name a move from your study material.
Wrong line: that move isn't in your selected openings. Reset and go again.
Not from your selected opening lines, so go again. The study changed, so this saved attempt doesn't affect its review schedule.
Outside your selected opening lines, so go again. This position is retired, and its review schedule stays as is.
Under mixed Due, moves from this line all count. Dedicated practice drills this line exclusively.
Scheduled recalls drill the moves of your chosen side. A position shared by your active studies uses one card.
Reload the saved session, then carry on.
Verified line, running on the board now.
Revealed, and logged that way. Solution available for replay below.
Second attempt, full solution! Miss and finish: both go in the log.
Full solution, zero wrong moves. Flawless execution!
Negative on that move for this puzzle. Everything correct so far is logged.
Affirmative! Next objective: the following move.
Work out the line first. Commit after that.
Not enough from the engine to explain this position. No guessing.
Review standing by. Hit resume below, or take a piece out on patrol.
Choose any move to inspect, or move a piece and run your own test.
Straight from the manual: a book move.
This move is in the field manual: standard opening drill. Proceed.
It's in the manual, under a recognized opening line.
Still following the manual.
The manual supplies another move. Carry on.
Even the reply is straight from the manual.
The manual is still in charge. Steady.
Manual still open. Formation holds.
Still marching to the book's beat.
The drill continues: another book move.
The manual still covers it. Book status tells you where we stand, not what the move is worth.
Briefing begins now! Advance move by move, and flag anything that looks out of line.
Waffles, reporting for duty! Your games are the mission. We find the weak spots, and we fix them.
Battle stations! Today the enemy is me, and I fully intend to win. Hold your ground, and make me fight for every inch!
Bold maneuver! A piece thrown into the breach, and capturing it does not win the day. Outstanding!
Brilliant! Material sent over the top, and the checked line backs the charge.
Medal-worthy! A ribbon for this sacrifice: real material given, and it holds when taken.
Commander's move! Into the record books with this one: a sacrifice that keeps its footing under fire.
Battle-tested! The fight hit a critical point here, and this move is a strong one.
Decoration earned! Stakes high on the field, and this move delivers.
Great move! A strong order, given at a moment that counted.
Right call at the right time! That's how campaigns are won.
Top choice! Straight down the line.
Best move. Orders followed to the letter.
Dead center! Nothing on this field outranks it.
Precision strike! No ground given up at all.
Holding formation. Not the sharpest move, but sound.
Good move. Acceptable; a sharper route was on the map.
Steady! The top choice was a step ahead, and very little was given away.
Within range! Close to the top orders, not quite on them.
Slightly off course! A small drift, but a drift.
Light damage reported! An inaccuracy, entered in the log.
Minor skirmish. The line bends a little here; it doesn't break.
Inaccuracy! A few inches of ground conceded on this move.
Misfire! A real mistake, and the cost is well beyond a slip.
Negative! That's a real error. Back to the map and find the better route.
Error confirmed! That order gives up a hefty slice of value.
Breach in the line! That move gives up ground that matters. Flag it for review.
There was a gap in the lines, and this move marches right past it!
Opportunity missed! A window was open, and this move didn't go through it.
Chance in range, and this move holds fire.
Miss! This turn held a real objective, and the move reports to a different post.
Halt! A serious blunder, and the price is steep. Mark this position, first priority!
Major blunder! The whole front swung on that move. Full inspection, now!
Blunder! One order, and the position suffers a severe setback.
Big shake-up on the field! That move costs dearly, and every unit feels the hit.
Legal move, wrong route for this lesson. Regroup and redeploy.
Affirmative! That's the lesson's move.
Lesson move on the board. Take note, recruit!
Stand by and watch the line advance.
Drill call: execute the studied move.
Side mission open. Scout it out, then report back to the main line.
Chapter complete, progress logged. Mission accomplished!
Full game on the table. Inspect it at your own pace.
Lesson down! Reload to get back in formation.
